claims.text: The U.S. Air Force fact sheet states: 'The Tacit Blue (Whale) aircraft was built to test the advances in stealth technology. The USAF, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, and the Northrop Corp. worked together from 1978 to 1985 to demonstrate that curved surfaces on an aircraft result in a low radar return signal from ground radar.'

claims.text: The same fact sheet: 'The aircraft made its first flight in February 1982, and by the conclusion of the program in 1985, had flown 135 times. It had a digital fly-by-wire flight control system to help stabilize the aircraft. Tacit Blue had a single flush inlet on the top of the fuselage to provide air to its two engines. The aircraft was placed on display at the museum in May 1996.'

Armament: None.' Five pilots are named on a plaque mounted in the cockpit: Mr. Richard Thomas, Col. (Sel) Don Cornell, Lt. Col. Russ Easter, Lt. Col. Ken Dyson and Maj. Dan Vanderhorst.

claims.text: Stated inference, and it is recorded against the brief that asked for the opposite. No source was opened arguing that the TR-3B narrative derives from or is confused with TACIT BLUE, and the primary record argues against it: the fact sheet's defining feature is curved surfaces, the aircraft is 48 feet across against a claimed 200 to 600, and it was retired in 1985 against a craft claimed to have first flown in the early 1990s. There is no shape, size or date correspondence. The conflation the record does support is with the F-117, which is Peter Merlin's identification of the airframe in Fouche's own misattributed photograph.

desc: TACIT BLUE is on this board as the control case for the TR-3B, and its edge to the claim is a denial edge and not a supporting one. It is a real black programme of the right era, run by the right agencies, and its published record is precisely what the claim is not. The U.S. Air Force's own fact sheet states that 'The USAF, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, and the Northrop Corp. worked together from 1978 to 1985 to demonstrate that curved surfaces on an aircraft result in a low radar return signal from ground radar.' The aircraft made its first flight in February 1982 and had flown 135 times by the conclusion of the programme in 1985. It was placed on museum display in May 1996. Its span is 48 feet 2 inches, its length 55 feet 10 inches, its height 10 feet 7 inches, its weight 30,000 pounds, its powerplant two Garrett ATF3-6 high-bypass turbofans, and its armament none. THE POINT OF THE NODE: it is not triangular, its defining feature is curved surfaces, it is 48 feet across rather than 200 to 600, and it was retired before the TR-3B is claimed to have flown. The brief that produced this build asked for the widely reported analysis that the TR-3B narrative derives from or is confused with TACIT BLUE; that analysis was searched for and NOT FOUND, and the primary record argues against it. The documented aircraft that is close to triangular in planform and that did fly out of Groom Lake in the period is the F-117, which is the airframe Peter Merlin identifies in Fouche's own misattributed photograph.
